title: Nanak's twelve months
hook: Guru Nanak's own twelve months, older and more stark than Guru Arjan's (Tukhari, ang 1107)

segments.voice: Yesterday the Babarvani closed, and your line was faith that sees. Which hard story did you stop for? Today the same poet turns from a burning town to the turning year. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

What month is it? The quick answer comes off a phone screen: a name, a number, a box on a grid. But there's an older way of naming time in the Punjab, a calendar of months called Chet and Vaisakh, Savan and Poh, each with its own weather. Guru Nanak took that calendar and wrote a poem through it, a Barah Maha, twelve months of a soul missing its Beloved. You met it once on this path, in a single glance. Now we walk through it slowly, season by season, over the next few days. Today, before a single flower opens: how the poem begins, and how it sounds. Nanak's twelve months.
screen: `WHAT MONTH IS IT?` → `A CALENDAR WITH WEATHER.` → `NANAK'S TWELVE MONTHS.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. The poem sits in Raga Tukhari, on ang eleven hundred seven of the Guru Granth Sahib, under Guru Nanak's name. And it doesn't start with spring. It starts with a word to the listener: listen. Given here in plain English, not word for word: hear this. Each one lives out the deeds done before. On every head comes joy or sorrow, and whatever You give is good. Then the bride speaks. This world is Yours, Lord, so what is my state? Without You I can't live even a moment. That's the frame. Before any month is named, we're told who is speaking and what she lacks. Every season that follows is seen through that lack. Second, the sound. Each month gets its own long stanza, and the stanzas don't hurry. They pile up sights and sounds: blossoms, bees, a blazing sun, lightning, frost. Then they turn, again and again, to the same ache. The Beloved is not home. Third, the voice. The Granth holds another Barah Maha too, by Guru Arjan, in Raga Majh, and this path read it in year two. Both are true to the same longing. Some readers find Nanak's the starker of the two: the weather is heavier, the bride's cry more raw, the comfort held back until late. Put it simply, and the poem is a year in which nothing outside changes much, while everything inside is waiting. So for the coming days, each season gets its turn. Spring, the heat, the rains, the cold. And a name for all of it, today's line: Nanak's months.
screen: `IT OPENS WITH: LISTEN.` · `WHATEVER YOU GIVE IS GOOD.` · `EACH MONTH, THE SAME ACHE.` · `A STARKER VOICE, SOME SAY.` · then, large: `NANAK'S MONTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: note this month's name. If you can, look up the month you're in on the Punjabi calendar, the one the poem uses. If you can't right now, just use the name you know. Then sit with it. Say the name once, quietly. Let your breath slow. Notice the weather this month has brought: the light at the window, the air on your skin, what's growing or falling outside. Then ask, gently, what you're waiting for this month. Don't solve it. Just name it beside the month's name. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each slow breath. The bell holds the time.
Nanak's twelve months. Guru Nanak's Barah Maha in Raga Tukhari, which opens by asking us to listen, then walks the year through a bride's longing. Today's word.
Your line: nanak's months. Today, write this month's name somewhere you'll see it, and under it, one thing it's teaching you to wait for. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Barah Maha is sung in kirtan in Raga Tukhari and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib.

fork.setup: you're about to sing twelve months of longing. how does Guru Nanak's poem begin?
options: with a call to listen, and a word on deeds and what God gives.
fork.reveal: it opens with 'listen': each lives out past deeds, joy or sorrow comes, and whatever You give is good. only then do the months begin.

original.note: barah maha: twelve months, the heading over Guru Nanak's poem in Tukhari.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calendar poem about the seasons.
what it means: a year seen through one longing; the weather changes, the waiting doesn't.
what a scholar hears: Nanak frames the months with deeds and grace before Chet begins, so the seasons are read through hukam, what God gives.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Tukhari, Mahala 1, Barah Maha, opening stanza, Ang 1107 (listen; deeds done before; joy or sorrow; what You give is good; without You I can't live a moment)
Guru Granth Sahib, Majh, Mahala 5, Barah Maha, Ang 133–136 (Guru Arjan's twelve months, named only)

notes: The opening stanza (ਤੂ ਸੁਣਿ ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰੰਮਾ ਪੁਰਬਿ ਕਮਾਇਆ ... ਹਰਿ ਬਿਨੁ ਘੜੀ ਨ ਜੀਵਾ) is paraphrased; please confirm the reading.

The outline calls Nanak's months 'older and more stark' than Guru Arjan's. Per the claims rule the script does not say 'older'; it says 'some readers find Nanak's the starker of the two'. A Keeper may restore the comparison if wanted.
Month names Chet, Vaisakh, Savan, Poh are used as in the poem; the script does not map them to Western months.
Day 1109 already gave an overview of this poem, including its blessed-months ending; this day avoids the ending and focuses on the opening frame.
howItsDone: 'some Sikhs read the stanza for the month they're in' is a soft claim; please confirm or cut.

Editor pass: added the missing 'First' so the teach's steps run in order; cut howItsDone's claim that Nanak's stanzas are read as each month begins (the Sangrand custom is tied to Guru Arjan's Majh Barah Maha, as day 1168 says).
